notes: Veterinary study: all 24 deposited K. pneumoniae are from companion animals (dogs, cats, horses) and veterinary hospital environments at University of Liverpool (SAH1 small animal hospital, EH equine hospital) plus two external UK facilities (SAH2, SAP). Per rubric, non-human hosts at veterinary hospitals remain community; this applies equally to environmental isolates from veterinary (not human) hospital surfaces. ENA total=24 equals taxon=24, consistent with only K. pneumoniae deposited; P. aeruginosa WGS data are cited under the same accession in the paper but are absent from ENA or not counted (we grade Klebsiella only). Isolation sources are genuinely mixed across clinical body sites (wounds, urine, blood, surgical sites, skin), faecal/carriage, and environmental hospital surfaces — no single predominant source at ~95%. Hosts are likewise mixed (dogs predominate clinically but horses, cats, and environmental samples are substantial). Collection dates span 2012–2019 per Table 1 (K87, 21/06/2012, is earliest; K88–K92 cluster at 04/07/2019 is latest).

coverage_basis: Klebsiella (the taxon of interest) is not mentioned anywhere in the paper text. The paper covers phase variable epigenetic invertons in B. fragilis, E. faecalis, S. agalactiae, T. denticola, and S. pneumoniae. The EBI study title 'Phase_variable_epigenetic_control_in_firmicutes' and description (S. pneumoniae Type I R-M phase variation) likewise contain no Klebsiella content. The ENA reports 24 Klebsiella samples in this accession; these are entirely unaccounted for by this paper. Paper coverage for Klebsiella = 0/24 = 0%.
notes: Critical finding: the 24 Klebsiella samples in PRJEB17888 are entirely absent from this paper. The paper characterises phase variable epigenetic invertons in Firmicutes/Bacteroidetes/Spirochaetes organisms (B. fragilis, E. faecalis, S. agalactiae, T. denticola, S. pneumoniae); Klebsiella is a Proteobacterium and is not mentioned. The EBI study description explicitly frames the project around S. pneumoniae Type I R-M phase variation. The paper deposits SMRT and RNA-seq data to PRJNA593863 and PRJNA400682 (NCBI), not to PRJEB17888, suggesting PRJEB17888 is an early Wellcome Sanger pre-publication accession whose Klebsiella content is unrelated to or predates this paper. Paper coverage for Klebsiella = 0%. All Klebsiella-specific study-level attributes and backfill fields are not_gradeable. Although the paper does involve genetic engineering of S. pneumoniae expression strains (deletion knockouts + heterologous hsdS expression followed by SMRT sequencing), this cannot be attributed to the uncharacterised Klebsiella samples, so study_type is classified 'other' rather than experimental_evolution. The text was truncated but the omitted content is unlikely to include Klebsiella given the study's entire focus on Firmicutes/Bacteroidetes.

Country = Netherlands is supported by multiple local Dutch suppliers cited in the methods section (Senzora BV Deventer, Diversey Utrecht, Jojoli Barendrecht). Isolation source and host cannot be proposed as a single value since the outbreak investigation sampled both patients (blood, urine, rectal swabs) and hospital environment (sink/shower drains, toilets), and the Klebsiella-specific subset is undefined.

study_setting.evidence_quote: Fresh, cooled, native stool samples from a cohort of adults (MikroResist, n=59) and children (MikroKids, n=54) ... All human donors have signed a letter of informed consent in accordance with the World Medical Association Declaration of Helsinki

cohort_age.evidence_quote: in 23 individuals, with 19 isolates from children (MK1-19) and four isolates from adults (MR1-4)

coverage_basis: The paper explicitly describes exactly 23 K. oxytoca isolates recovered and genome-sequenced (MK01–MK19 from the MikroKids child cohort and MR01–MR04 from the MikroResist adult cohort), matching the ENA taxon count of 23 exactly. The deposited data section confirms 'K. oxytoca genomes have been deposited ... under the accession number PRJEB42167'.

country.evidence_quote: Human sample and data collections have been performed in agreement with the guidelines of the Helmholtz Center for Infection Research, Braunschweig, Germany, the Ethics Committee Lower Saxony (permit No. 8629_BO_K_2019; No. 8750_BO_K_2019)

isolation_source.evidence_quote: Isolation of commensal Klebsiella strains from human stool samples: Stool samples were homogenized in 1 mL PBS and plated in serial dilutions on Simmons Citrate Agar plates supplemented with inositol, tryptophan and bile salts (SCITB)

host.evidence_quote: selective plating and species-specific PCR screening revealed the presence of K. oxytoca in 23 individuals, with 19 isolates from children (MK1-19) and four isolates from adults (MR1-4)

notes: SIZING: ENA reports 23 Klebsiella samples; the paper describes exactly 23 K. oxytoca isolates sequenced (MK01–MK19 + MR01–MR04) — a direct 1:1 match. The CRISPR-Cas9 deletion mutants (DcasA, DbglX) created during the study are not among the 23 deposited genomes. STUDY TYPE: Although the paper includes CRISPR knockout experiments, the 23 deposited genomes are naturally-isolated commensal K. oxytoca strains from healthy human donors (observational); the CRISPR work was a downstream functional assay, not the subject of the deposit. AMR_STUDY: The K. oxytoca isolates were selected by species identity alone (SCITB agar morphology + K. oxytoca pehX-gene PCR); ampicillin plating exploited intrinsic species-level resistance as a practical filter, not an acquired-AMR gate — classified surveillance. AMR_TARGET and AMR_METHOD are therefore not applicable. COHORT_AGE: 19/23 isolates from children and 4/23 from adults → mixed. COUNTRY: Helmholtz Center Braunschweig; Lower Saxony ethics committee; both human cohorts recruited in Germany. COLLECTION_DATE: no explicit collection year or date range is stated in the full text.

coverage_basis: No paper text available; study is described as a pre-publication release from the Wellcome Trust Sanger Institute. All grading is based solely on the EBI study title and description.
notes: This is a clear experimental_evolution study: laboratory strains of K. pneumoniae (B5055 and ATCC43816) were deliberately exposed to bacteriophage infection to select phage-resistant mutant colonies, which were then sequenced to characterise the mutations conferring resistance. This is directly analogous to culturing in antibiotic broth to drive resistance mutations. Per the rubric, this study should be EXCLUDED from the cohort. The isolates are not clinical or environmental samples — they are lab strains undergoing directed experimental evolution. No AMR selection was applied; the selection criterion was bacteriophage resistance. No paper is available (pre-publication release); no country, host, isolation_source, or collection_date can be determined from the EBI description. The Wellcome Trust Sanger Institute is cited as the depositor but institutional affiliation does not establish collection country per rubric rules, and in any case these are reference lab strains with no meaningful 'collection country.'

study_type.evidence_quote: Characterisation of these phage resistant colonies would aid in identifying 'escape' routes for bacteria during phage infection. It would also allow us to complement and compare data we will generate in future upon infection of a TraDIS library of K. pneumoniae ATCC43816 mutants. We may expect point mutations as well as possible fragment loss or combination of both. Illumina Sequencing will thus help to pin down these DNA changes.

COHORT_AGE: Not reported.

notes: SIZING: Pattern B — paper covers two accessions (PRJNA577535 + PRJNA751707); the paper's sequenced Klebsiella total (46) substantially exceeds this accession's ENA count (17). notes: PRJEB45397 contains bacterial genome sequences and metagenomic data from a paediatric IBD microbiome study at Monash Children's Hospital, Victoria, Australia. All 15 ENA samples are Klebsiella (ena_taxon_samples = ena_total_samples = 15). The study WGS 745 phylogenetically diverse isolates selected from 6,620 cultured from mucosal biopsies; the 15 Klebsiella in ENA are a small taxon-specific subset (Case B sizing pattern — full 745-genome corpus likely spans multiple accessions). notes: SIZING: ENA reports 14 Klebsiella = 14 total samples. Paper tabulates 6 K. pneumoniae from Libyan patients + 5 K. pneumoniae from hospital environment (all environmental Enterobacteriaceae were K. pneumoniae) + 4 K. pneumoniae from Syrian patients = 15; discrepancy of 1 is minor and likely reflects one sample not deposited. Coverage ~100%, well above 75% threshold; all study-level attributes can be graded on the whole project. AMR_STUDY=amr: every isolate qualified by meeting the MDR definition (3GC or carbapenem resistance); susceptible controls were not added. AMR_TARGET=other: the formal selection criterion is composite—'resistance against third-generation methoxyimino cephalosporins OR carbapenems'—combining both 3GC and carbapenem targets; it is not reducible to a single listed category (the majority of Klebsiella are ESBL/3GC-resistant but the formal criterion also admits carbapenems and MRSA, and the study is explicitly defined as MDR). AMR_METHOD=ast_result: VITEK 2 phenotypic AST drove inclusion; PCR was used for subsequent characterisation, not for primary selection. COHORT_AGE=mixed: Syrian patient WEST-S3 was 4 years old; all others are adults (range 4–52). COUNTRY=Germany (all isolations performed at German Bundeswehr hospitals). ISOLATION_SOURCE: no single source approaches 95%—Libyan-patient Klebsiella predominantly from inguinal skin; Syrian-patient Klebsiella from perineal skin, wound, superficial wound at groin; environmental Klebsiella from hands, walking frame, bag handle. HOST: ~13/15 Klebsiella derive from humans (10 patient isolates + 3 environmental 'hands'/'hands and beard'); 2 are from inanimate surfaces (walking frame, bag handle)—13% exception rate exceeds the small-minority threshold for applies_whole_project, so proposed_value=human but applies_whole_project=false. COLLECTION_DATE: Libya cohort admitted 2011, Syria cohort 2013; span 2011–2013.

notes: SIZING (Pattern B): ENA shows 10 total samples, all Klebsiella, from the West Africa/Ibadan node (PRJEB58695). The SeqAfrica paper describes 18,264 bacterial genomes across five regional hubs — the article's sequenced count vastly exceeds E=10, confirming this accession is one of many ENA deposits from the broader project. Paper coverage for this specific accession is effectively zero. AMR_STUDY graded 'surveillance' from the EBI study description, which uses explicit surveillance language and describes pathogen-level selection (priority AMR species) rather than per-isolate resistance phenotype gating. The project's decision-tree criteria (priority pathogen type, public health utility) do not require each isolate to have a resistant phenotype. STUDY_SETTING not gradeable: the EBI description covers multiple West African source countries and the paper explicitly reports samples from human clinical (90%), animal (5%), and environmental (2%) sectors across all hubs — the setting for these 10 specific Klebsiella samples cannot be determined. COUNTRY not gradeable: multiple West African countries submit to the Ibadan hub and no single country of collection can be attributed. HOST proposed as 'human' (90% of all project genomes were human clinical) but applies_whole_project=false since 90% falls below the ~95% threshold and the specific provenance of these 10 samples is unknown. COLLECTION_DATE spans project phase 1: 2019–2023.

country.evidence_quote: Two carbapenem-resistant strains (C182 and C248, ST11 clones) and one colistin-resistant strain (HK1) were obtained from a national surveillance program in China.

isolation_source.evidence_quote: Chromosome Abdominal wound secretions isolated mcr-1 producing Klebsiella pneumoniae HK1 and its tigecycline resistant mutants sequencing

host.evidence_quote: the bacterial strains used in this study were obtained from clinical specimens with fully anonymised, nontraceable patient information

collection_date.evidence_quote: HK1 — Female/71, Abdominal wound secretions, 2011 (Table 1)

raw.notes: EXCLUDED: study_type = experimental_evolution. The EBI description explicitly states 'in vitro molecular evolution… experimental evolution', and the paper describes in vitro serial passage under a stepwise tigecycline gradient plus CRISPR-Cas9 gene knockouts (ramA, rarA, lon, combinations) to drive resistance mutations — both criteria that define experimental_evolution under the rubric. All 10 ENA samples are Klebsiella. The parent HK1 was a clinical isolate from abdominal wound secretions (2011, China, hospital patient); the remaining samples are in vitro evolved tigecycline-resistant mutants or CRISPR-knockout derivatives, for which isolation_source and host are not applicable (in vitro is not a valid source/host). study_setting is not_gradeable because the deposited genomes are predominantly in vitro-created strains with no applicable care setting. cohort_age is not_gradeable as this is a pure microbiology in vitro experiment with no human subjects. amr_study is graded 'amr' because all isolates entered the project via AMR attributes (mcr-1 colistin resistance for HK1; tigecycline MIC elevation for evolved mutants). amr_target is 'other' (tigecycline). amr_method is ast_result (MIC up to 256 mg/L used to confirm tigecycline resistance in evolved mutants, the majority of deposited samples). Country backfill China applies to all 10 samples. isolation_source and host backfills do not apply to the whole project since most samples are in vitro-evolved.
